title: The Sacred Heart at home
hookLine: families place an image of the Sacred Heart in the home

lines: I STAND AT THE GATE, AND KNOCK.
cards: "Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock." That's Christ speaking in the Bible's last book, the one the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse, and the next line says what happens if someone opens.
Some Catholic families take that line almost literally. They hang a picture where the family actually lives and invite him in, on purpose, with a small ceremony.

teach.h: AN IMAGE IN A PLACE OF HONOR.
teach.b: The practice has a formal name: enthronement. A family chooses a picture or statue of the Sacred Heart, Jesus pointing to his heart, and gives it a place of honor: the living room, the kitchen wall, above the table.
Not a closet, not a hallway nobody uses. It's meant to be seen in the ordinary traffic of family life. A priest may come to bless the image.
The family gathers, prays together, and consecrates the household to the Sacred Heart: a promise to treat Christ as the head of the home.
Some families sign a certificate, hang it nearby, and renew the consecration each year on the feast.
Tradition links all this to Margaret Mary, who wrote that Jesus promised to bless the places where an image of his heart is set up and honored.

teach.h: I WILL COME IN AND SUP WITH HIM.
teach.b: The full verse, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. If any man shall hear my voice, and open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me."

To sup is to eat supper. So the picture isn't decoration, and it isn't a guard dog. It's a reminder that a guest has been invited to the table: to the arguments, the homework, the overdue bills, the birthday cake.
Last, what it asks of the household. Hanging an image is easy.

Living under it is harder. The hope is that the picture works quietly over time: a sharp word swallowed because he's looking; a short grace before a meal that used to be eaten standing at the counter.
One glance at the wall says it: he lives here.

how: Some Catholic families enthrone an image of the Sacred Heart in a central room of the house, usually with a blessing by a priest and a family act of consecration, and renew it on the feast of the Sacred Heart.

games.q: what does “the sacred heart at home” mean?
o: a heart-shaped charm hung for good luck
a blessed image of Christ's heart in the home
a statue kept only in a church sanctuary

games.q: the Sacred Heart at home — tap the pairs.
p: an image given a place of honor
Christ as head of the home

s: the image is meant to be kept somewhere private
it goes where family life happens: the living room, the kitchen, near the table.
in the Apocalypse, Christ knocks and promises to come in and eat
"I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me."
the Sacred Heart image works as a guard against harm
it's a reminder of an invited guest, not a charm.

games.q: your family is enthroning the Sacred Heart. where does the image go?
o: a spare closet, so it stays safe.
where the family actually lives, like the kitchen.
the front porch, facing the street.
games.why: a place of honor in the middle of family life. the guest is invited to the table, not stored away.

practice: If there's a Sacred Heart picture or any holy image in your home, stand before it, or bring it to mind, and look at it as if for the first time.

If you pray, make the sign of the cross toward it and ask God to bless everyone who walks past it. If there's no image, think about where one would go: the room where your household really lives, not the room that's tidy.

wordCard.voice: The Sacred Heart at home. An image of Christ's heart honored where a family lives, with the household consecrated to him: a standing invitation to a guest at the table.

orig.note: Latin: heart of Jesus, the words that open the invocations of the Litany of the Sacred Heart.

carryVoice: Your line: he lives here. A guest for arguments and birthday cake alike. Same time tomorrow.
